chunks: Design an opto-isolated gate drive. The question: Describe/draw/design an opto-isolation circuit.
An opto-isolated gate drive lets a microcontroller switch a power transistor with no electrical connection between them. The pin lights an LED.
A phototransistor (a transistor switched by light) on the other side sees it, and a small buffer stage then pushes current into the power FET's gate.
You size the LED resistor, size the output stage for an aged part, make the buffer fast enough to charge the gate, and choose the polarity so a reset leaves the FET off.
Picture a person flashing a small lamp to tell a crane operator across a yard to lift. The lamp signal is weak and the crane needs real power.
So the operator uses the signal to work a big lever. The phototransistor's weak output is the lamp signal, and the buffer transistors are the big lever.
The crane also needs its own power: an isolated supply.
GPIO high drives I F equals (3. 3-1. 2) over 200 equals 10. 5 milliamps. The pin low, or high-impedance at reset, means no current: LED off. This is the default-safe polarity.
LED series resistor ( R LED ): sets the LED current, (V pin minus V F) over I F .
End-of-life CTR: the lowest transfer ratio the part will have after aging and heat; the value to design with.
Emitter follower: a transistor stage whose output copies its input voltage and can supply more current.
Isolated supply: a power source for the output side that shares no conductor with the microcontroller side.
Gate pulldown: a resistor that holds the FET off if nothing drives the gate.
A 3. 3 volts pin drives the LED at 10 milliamps, so R LED equals (3. 3 minus 1. 2) over 10 milliamps equals 210 ohms, and you use 200 ohms.
At 20% end-of-life CTR the phototransistor passes 0. 2 times 10. 5 equals 2. 1 milliamps. A plain pull-up of 5. 6 kilohms feeding a 2 nanofarads gate has a time constant of 5.
6 k times 2 nanofarads equals 11 microseconds, far too slow, and it is also inverting.
So use an emitter-follower output, which is non-inverting and off by default, then add a buffer stage. That is the whole idea.
"I'd bias the LED at about 10 milliamps from the GPIO: (3. 3 minus 1. 2)/10 milliamps is 210 ohms, so 200 ohms, active-high so reset means off.

On the output side I'd run the phototransistor from an isolated 12 volts as an emitter follower into a pulldown, which is non-inverting, defaults off and goes to about 11 volts at end-of-life CTR, then buffer it with an NPN/PNP pair into a 10 ohms gate resistor with a gate-source pulldown, because a plain pull-up into a gate is microseconds slow.
Then verify CTR margin, delays and CMTI."
Quick check.
What is the main reason to use the phototransistor as an emitter follower (collector to supply, emitter to a pulldown) instead of a pull-up on the collector for gate drive?
